title: Cimarron Hills Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Cimarron Hills wells have a 140 ft median depth, with local drilling costs shaped by Denver Basin ground conditions.
h1: Cimarron Hills Colorado Well Depth, Yield, and Cost
intro_html:
For rural properties around Cimarron Hills, the local well records point to moderate typical depths but a wide spread from one lot to the next. The median reported depth is 140 feet, while the middle half runs from 50 to 389 feet. Most wells are tied to the Denver Basin, including unnamed fractured-bedrock formations, Arapahoe, and Denver aquifers.

That range matters when you are pricing a property or preparing a building budget. A nearby well is useful evidence, but it does not guarantee the same depth, yield, or water quality on your parcel. Check the DWR permit record, neighboring well construction, and the intended household or irrigation use before committing to a site.

sections.heading: Cimarron Hills well depths vary across the Denver Basin
sections.html:
Of the local records that report depth, the middle half of wells is 50 to 389 feet, with a median of 140 feet. About 43% are under 100 feet, 21% fall from 100 to 300 feet, and 28% reach 300 to 600 feet. Another 8% are deeper than 600 feet. The deepest recorded well is 1,840 feet.

This is a wide bidding range for a driller. A 140-foot estimate may be reasonable for early budgeting, but a parcel near a deeper local cluster could require a very different bid. Ground conditions here are Denver Basin sedimentary bedrock, with many permits naming fractured-bedrock or Denver Basin aquifers. Neighboring construction reports are more useful than a countywide average when setting expectations.

sections.heading: Most Cimarron Hills wells make usable household yields
sections.html:
Reported well yields are comparatively strong in this dataset. The median is 10.0 gallons per minute, and the middle half runs from 8.0 to 12.0 gallons per minute. About 76% of reported yields are between 5 and 15 gallons per minute, while 19% report more than 15 gallons per minute. The records show 0% under 1 gallon per minute and 5% from 1 to 5 gallons per minute.

Those figures describe tested well performance, not a guaranteed daily supply. A household-use well still needs an appropriate pump, pressure tank, storage, and electrical system. Ask for the actual well test and construction report rather than relying only on a listing statement. If you plan substantial irrigation, livestock use, or another non-household purpose, confirm the permit conditions and water rights before buying.

sections.heading: Recorded water levels are shallower in newer measurements
sections.html:
The median static water level in the available records is 53 feet below ground surface, with the middle half from 35 to 93 feet. The decade series shows a median of 210 feet in the 1980s, 66 feet in the 2010s, and 47 feet in the 2020s.

That pattern does not show a dropping water table in these records. Newer measurements are shallower, but the measurements may come from different wells, aquifers, seasons, and testing conditions. Only 103 local wells report a static water level, so the series is not a complete monitoring network. For a purchase, compare the measurement date, well depth, aquifer, and pumping history. A current water-level check is more useful than assuming the decade medians apply directly to your lot.

sections.heading: Cimarron Hills permit activity and local drillers
sections.html:
The DWR record includes 2,503 wells within 5 miles of Cimarron Hills, with 1,296 recorded as constructed. Permits span from the 1950s through a newest permit year of 2025. Permit activity was highest in the 1990s, with 445 permits issued, followed by 290 in the 2000s and 287 in the 1980s.

The most active names in these records are Authorized (Pe, Pg), Hamacher Well Works Inc (Hamacher, Alan Ray), and M & B Drilling Co. (Mateyka, John E.). These records help identify local experience, but they are not a recommendation or proof that a contractor is available for your project. Confirm current licensing, insurance, scope, and the proposed casing, grout, pump, testing, and permit work in writing.

sections.heading: What a new Cimarron Hills well may cost
sections.html:
The local drilling model uses a typical rate of $50 to $70 per foot in Denver Basin sedimentary bedrock. At the 140-foot median depth, the drilled hole works out to about $7,000 to $9,800. A finished system, including the pump, tank, trenching, and electrical, is modeled at about $13,000 to $21,800.

That is a planning range, not a fixed quote. Depth is the largest early variable, and the local range extends from shallow wells to a recorded 1,840 feet. Ask whether the bid includes mobilization, casing, grout, development, water testing, pump installation, pressure equipment, trenching, and electrical. Also ask how the contractor handles a low-yield or dry hole. Compare bids on the same scope so a low per-foot number does not hide unfinished system work.

sections.heading: Environmental and building checks before you buy
sections.html:
Records within about 10 miles include 169 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 22 historic mine features, and 52 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Their presence does not prove contamination on a particular parcel, but it is a reason to check the well location, nearby land uses, and available water-quality data. Test existing water before closing and plan appropriate follow-up testing for a new well.

Also verify septic setbacks, soil conditions, access for a drilling rig, and the intended house location before purchasing. A permit may be for domestic or household use, stock, irrigation, or monitoring; the local mix is 50% domestic or household, 4% stock, 2% irrigation, and 30% monitoring. Colorado DWR rules control what an exempt household-use well can serve, and an augmentation plan may be needed in an over-appropriated basin for uses outside the permit.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Cimarron Hills?
faq.a: The median reported well depth near Cimarron Hills is 140 feet. The middle half runs from 50 to 389 feet, so nearby properties can differ substantially. About 43% of wells are under 100 feet, while 8% are deeper than 600 feet. The deepest recorded well is 1,840 feet.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Cimarron Hills?
faq.a: The local cost model uses $50 to $70 per foot. At the 140-foot median depth, drilling the hole is estimated at $7,000 to $9,800. A finished system with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $13,000 to $21,800. A driller should provide a detailed scope because depth varies widely.

faq.q: How much water do wells produce in Cimarron Hills?
faq.a: The median reported yield is 10.0 gallons per minute, with the middle half from 8.0 to 12.0 gallons per minute. About 76% of reported yields are between 5 and 15 gallons per minute, and 19% exceed 15 gallons per minute. Review the actual well test and permit before relying on a yield claim.

faq.q: Is well water safe in Cimarron Hills?
faq.a: Safety cannot be determined from depth or yield alone. Within about 10 miles, records identify 169 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 22 historic mine features, and 52 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Test an existing well before closing and test a new well after construction, using the site history to guide the water-quality panel.

faq.q: Should I check a neighboring well before buying land near Cimarron Hills?
faq.a: Yes. The local records include 2,503 wells within 5 miles, but only 1,458 report total depth, 377 report pump yield, and 103 report static water level. Neighboring reports can show likely depth, aquifer, yield, and water level, but they do not guarantee the same result on your parcel. Confirm the permit and intended use with Colorado DWR.
